title: A yearly pilgrimage
hook: go somewhere holy once a year
tomorrow: three days with no phone: rest, or punishment?

segments.voice: Yesterday's line: faith you can taste, with a plate saved for the empty table. Today the feast is at the end of a road.
screen: `FAITH YOU CAN TASTE.` → `A FEAST AT THE END OF A ROAD.`

segments.voice: The family chat lights up: the yearly trip is set, and it's the same weekend as the thing you've waited all season for. Same drive as always, same gas station, same aunt asleep in the back seat, same shrine at the end. Why walk to the same holy place every single year? It can feel like a rerun. Luke says Jesus's family made a trip like that too.
screen: `THE SAME WEEKEND, OF COURSE.` → `SAME DRIVE, SAME SHRINE.` → `WHY EVERY YEAR?`

segments.voice: In the Douay-Rheims: "And his parents went every year to Jerusalem, at the solemn day of the pasch." Every year, with a whole crowd of relatives and neighbors. Here's one to tell a friend: on the way home from one of those trips, Mary and Joseph lost Jesus for a day, because they assumed he was somewhere in the company. That's how big the group was. The road was shared. Pilgrims had songs for it. One psalm begins: "I rejoiced at the things that were said to me: We shall go into the house of the Lord." The joy starts at the invitation, before anyone arrives. The Catechism says pilgrimages call to mind our whole journey toward heaven, and are special times for renewing prayer. So why the same place every year? Because the place stays put and you don't. Every year you arrive carrying something different: a loss, a new job, a question. The shrine becomes a measuring stick. For a week like this one, with two good things on one weekend, the tradition offers two quiet gifts. A yearly pilgrimage can be planned, so it can move. And it's meant to be walked with people.
screen: `EVERY YEAR TO JERUSALEM.` · `LOST IN THE COMPANY.` · `WE SHALL GO INTO THE HOUSE.` · `THE PLACE STAYS; YOU CHANGE.` · then, large: `ONCE A YEAR.`

segments.voice: Stand up and walk slowly for one minute, across a room or down a hallway, as if the last few steps lead to a holy place. With each step, name one person you'd want walking beside you. If you pray, you can say the psalm's line: we shall go into the house of the Lord.
A yearly pilgrimage. A trip to a holy place, made again and again, with the people you walk beside. Today's word.
Pocket this one: once a year, the same road, and a different you each time. Day done.

howItsDone: Catholics make pilgrimages to shrines, cathedrals and holy places; some families and parishes go to the same shrine each year, often on a feast day, praying and singing on the way.

fork.setup: your parish's yearly walk to a shrine is Saturday. your little brother says it's boring: 'we went last year, same place.' what does today's lesson give you to say?
options: the place stays the same so you can see how you've changed.

fork.reveal: a yearly pilgrimage is the same road with a different you. Jesus's family made the same trip every year, together.

original.note: Latin: a traveler from abroad. the word English pilgrim grew from.

what it means: it can be a yearly road to a nearby holy place, walked with people, that shows you how you've changed.

chat.meaning: A yearly pilgrimage is planned and shared: the point is going to the holy place together, not the exact date.

psalm.meaning: a sacred song from the Bible's book of Psalms

shrine.meaning: a holy place people visit to pray
